Apache Flink — What the Project Talks About, and What It Is Actually About

Ten years, 40,000 tickets. Every ticket names a few topics — some are what the ticket is about, others are just the scenery. Counting mentions tells you what people talk about. Attention tells you what they are working on. The two drift apart, and the gap is the story.

1 · The Map
Each dot is a topic in one year. Left to right — how often it is mentioned. Bottom to top — how often it is the point of the ticket, not the background. Size — number of mentions. The dotted lines cut the map into four roles: core talked about a lot, and it's the subject · backdrop talked about a lot, but only as the scenery · niche rare, but when it shows up, it's the subject · margins. Drag the year. Trails follow the highlighted topics.

2015 — one subject and a big floor. The project has one clear subject, the streaming API. The runtime and the Java API are named in just as many tickets, but as the place where bugs happen, not what the bug is about. They start in the backdrop and never leave.

2020 — the core slips into the scenery. The Table API is now the most-mentioned topic in the tracker. And it is quietly slipping: from being what tickets were about (0.89) to being the surface other work is described on (0.61). Streaming slides further — by 2020 it has crossed into the backdrop: still named in hundreds of tickets a year, almost never the subject.

One climber. Release engineering steps out of the backdrop: from a side-note inside feature tickets (0.33) to a subject in its own right (0.65). Python is the niche that became core: rare for years, but when a ticket mentions PyFlink, that is what the ticket is about (0.97 in 2026).

And the runtime? Second most-mentioned topic in the whole project, attention flat at 0.2 for a decade. Count mentions and it looks like the #2 concern. Look at attention and it is the floor everyone stands on.

2 · Who Changed Role
Attention in a topic's first years (its first 50 mentions, at most four years) versus its last four (2023–2026). Red — the topic faded into the backdrop. Green — it became a subject in its own right. Only topics with at least 50 mentions in both windows. Diamonds — the same drift re-measured independently, one ticket–topic pair at a time (100 tickets per window, see §4c); where the diamond agrees with the dot, the drift is not an artifact of the ordering.
Caveat: 2014 is an imported backlog (919 Stratosphere issues loaded on one day), so an early window of "2014" describes the inherited code base rather than the project's first year.

The original core faded into scenery. Streaming 0.60 → 0.26, Table API 0.89 → 0.60, data model 0.58 → 0.30. None of them lost mentions — the Table API is still #1. They lost the spotlight: the project stopped working on them and started working through them. Java looks like a fourth case (0.39 → 0.15), but its early value rests on 141 tickets from 2014; sampled over 2014–2015 the drift shrinks to 0.24 → 0.15 and is not significant under either measurement. Java was never the subject — it is an anchor, like the runtime, not a story.

The plumbing stepped forward. Release engineering 0.33 → 0.65, dependencies 0.47 → 0.61, the REST API 0.33 → 0.52. In a young project these are side-notes inside feature tickets. In a mature one, they are the tickets.

What did not survive a second look. Two stories this chart seems to tell are not told on this page. SQL appears to rise (0.48 → 0.69) — but 86% of SQL tickets also carry the Table tag, and in the early years the model listed Table first; judged on its own, SQL was a subject from the start (0.93) and faded like the rest of the stack (→ 0.69). Test infrastructure appeared to rise (0.53 → 0.77) — until the imported 2014 backlog was removed, which leaves it flat (0.75 → 0.77); judged pair by pair it never leaves the lower half (0.27 → 0.40): a flaky test is a ticket about the component, and the test is the circumstance. Kubernetes shows no significant drift under either measurement. The three drifts above — streaming, Table, release engineering — reproduce under both; Java and the runtime stay low and flat under both, as anchors should.

3 · One Topic at a Time
Pick a topic. Blue — how often it is mentioned (share of that week's tickets, smoothed). Yellow — how much of those mentions are really about it. When the yellow line falls while the blue one rises, a subject is turning into scenery. The thin dotted line is the model's average score for the topic — it tells the same story, and is here only as a check.
4 · How We Measured, and What the Numbers Can't Tell You
We asked a language model to list each ticket's topics from most to least central, with a score from 0.1 to 1.0. The scores turned out to be a habit, not a measurement: the first topic gets 0.9 almost every time (86% of tickets), the second 0.8, then 0.5, then 0.3 — whatever the ticket says. So we never use the numbers. We use the ordering: which topics the model put in the top band (score 0.7 and above). That is what "attention" means on this page.
4a · Is the ruler steady? Share of topics in each band — top (0.7+), middle (0.4–0.7), low (below 0.4) — and topics per ticket, by year. Flat means the changes above are about the topics, not about the model drifting.
4b · The habit. The score given to the 1st, 2nd, … 5th topic of a ticket. Position decides the number.
4c · A second, independent measurement. The ordering above is relative: it says which of a ticket's topics comes first. To check it, we asked the same model to judge ticket–topic pairs one at a time, with no list to order — an absolute judgement. On 500 random tickets (1,664 pairs) the two agree on the top topic 83% of the time; the fixed 0.9/0.8/0.5 ladder dissolves (spread of the first score triples), and 500 control pairs with unrelated topics score 0.11 on average. Per-topic attention agrees at ρ = 0.68 — the pairwise judge is kinder to broad topics like the runtime and Java. Then we re-measured the drifts themselves, 100 early and 100 late tickets per topic:
A note on 2014. The tracker opens with 919 issues imported from the pre-Apache Stratosphere GitHub tracker on a single day (9 June 2014); 918 were already closed. They are 70% of the tickets dated 2014 and most of several topics' earliest observations. Treat 2014 as a snapshot of the inherited backlog, not as a year of activity.

"Semantic mass" is frequency in disguise. Sum up the scores per topic and you get something that looks like a measure of meaning. It tracks plain mention counts at 0.997 — and at 0.999 if you shuffle the scores at random. Any chart built on it would be a mention count with extra steps.

Attention is different. Across real topics it ranges from 0.10 to 0.94; shuffle the scores and the range collapses to 0.49–0.58. Which topic the model puts in the top band is a real, stable judgement about the topic — and it has nothing to do with how often the topic is mentioned. That independence is what makes the map readable.

This is not Flink being unusually tidy. Seventy percent of tickets have two or more top-band topics, and sub-tasks — the narrowest kind of ticket — have more of them than new features. The one-0.9-first pattern is the instrument, not the project.

5 · Where the Subject Went
Pick a topic. Left — with the ordering. Each year, the topic's mentions split into tickets where it is the subject (grey) and tickets led by some other topic, coloured by who leads. When a topic fades into the backdrop, this shows who took over: attention does not vanish, it moves. Right — the same tickets, tags as a plain set. No first topic, no grey band: all a binary tagging can say is which other topics appear alongside. Nothing is modelled in either panel; every band and line is a count of tickets.
Who is the subject — needs the ordering
Who is mentioned alongside — binary tags only
Why the ordering matters here. A set of tags can say that Table tickets increasingly mention SQL. It cannot say whether SQL joined the conversation or took it over — and for the runtime it will report that Table "rose" alongside it by 24 points when Table took the lead in only 5% more of its tickets. Co-mention is symmetric and inflates with every topic that grows everywhere; the subject role is one bit per ticket, and it is the bit that separates a neighbour from a successor.
Is there a time lag? If attention flowed from one topic to another, a burst in one should be followed by a burst in the other a few months later. We checked: monthly mention shares for the 40 largest topics, month-to-month changes, cross-correlated at lags of 1–6 months, against a null of time-shifted series. The handover above is a change in what tickets are about, not a wave that travels from topic to topic in time.
Appendix · Do the Scores Change Who Travels With Whom?
Six pairs of topics, quarter by quarter: how closely they appear together in the same tickets (distance = 1 − correlation, smoothed). Coloured — computed from the scores. Grey dashed — computed from plain presence, scores ignored. The two lines sit on top of each other in every panel. Whatever the scores add, it isn't here.

Growing together: SQL and the optimizer become inseparable (0.85 → 0.42); running on Kubernetes increasingly means configuring the runtime (1.01 → 0.77); Java and streaming, both now backdrop, travel as shared scenery (1.00 → 0.80).

Drifting apart: the Table API and Kubernetes are two success stories that have nothing to do with each other (1.03 → 1.20); data modelling left the Java API and moved to the Table side (0.68 → 0.85).
